Abstract
Purpose: To investigate the time and frequency dependence of diffusion kur-
tosis in the in vivo human brain with pulsed (PGSE) and oscillating gradient
spin-echo (OGSE) experiments over a range of diffusion times and frequencies
using high-performance gradients.
Methods: Four OGSE waveforms probing centroid frequencies of 11, 20, 34, and
51 Hz, corresponding to equivalent effective diffusion times of 22.7, 12.5, 7.4, and
4.9 ms; and three PGSE waveforms probing effective diffusion times of 50, 22.7,
and 12.5 ms were designed for experimentation. Seven healthy volunteers were
scanned using said waveforms at b-values of 500, 1000, and 2000 s/mm2. Kurtosis
metrics were computed and evaluated in various white and gray matter regions
of interest. Complementary Monte-Carlo simulations were performed using a
simple substrate with varying permeabilities and the same gradient waveforms
as used for in vivo imaging.
Results: Non-monotonic, biphasic kurtosis time- and frequency-dependences
were observed in different white and gray matter regions. This behavior supports
the notion that kurtosis is influenced by the combined effects of water-restriction
interactions, inter-compartmental water exchange, and tissue heterogeneity.
Kurtosis values measured using OGSE and PGSE waveforms at the same effec-
tive diffusion times showed significant discrepancies, with consistently higher
values from PGSE than OGSE. These discrepancies are mainly attributed to
differences in exchange sensitivities among gradient waveforms based on anal-
ogous findings from Monte-Carlo simulations.

INTRODUCTION
Diffusion
kurtosis
imaging
(DKI)
assesses
the
non-Gaussianity of diffusion of water molecules in bio-
logical tissues, providing additional microstructural tissue
information to conventional DTI.1,2 The derived dif-
fusion kurtosis is influenced by the interplay of tissue
characteristics such as the heterogeneity of diffusivity
within the imaging voxel, membrane restrictions of the
diffusive microenvironments, and inter-compartmental
water exchange between compartments with distinct
diffusivities.1–3 In addition to tissue characteristics, the
effective diffusion time (Δeff) probed by the employed
diffusion-encoding gradient waveform also affects kur-
tosis measurements.4 Over long diffusion times, the
effect of coarse-graining over structural disorder5,6 and
water exchange1,2,7,8 homogenizes the medium, thereby
reducing the degree of diffusion non-Gaussianity. Over
short diffusion times, tissue heterogeneity and interac-
tions between water molecules and restrictions become
more prominent; therefore, as diffusion time decreases,
increasingly sparse interactions lead to increasingly Gaus-
sian water diffusion.9,10 As such, kurtosis is understood
to exhibit a non-monotonic, biphasic time-dependence,
and studying such trend provides a new dimension for
exploring tissue microstructure.
Using Monte-Carlo (MC) simulations,11 the evolution
of kurtosis with respect to diffusion times has been exten-
sively investigated by employing tissue models with dif-
ferent levels of complexity.4,9,12–17 Through such simu-
lations, non-monotonic kurtosis time-dependences were
reported in multiple studies,4,9,12–16 wherein kurtosis first
increases with increasing diffusion time over a rela-
tively short time regime and then decreases as diffusion
time continues to increase. The rise time of the kurtosis
time-dependence curve to its peak (tpeak) with increasing
diffusion time has been recently demonstrated to correlate
with the membrane permeability and the size of the tissue
microstructure.12,16
Experimentally, the pulsed gradient spin-echo (PGSE)
sequence18 is commonly used for diffusion encoding over
different effective diffusion times. By varying the dura-
tion of each trapezoidal gradient pulse δ and the interval
between the monopolar pair of gradient pulses Δ, a range
of effective diffusion times approximately between 20 and
100 ms can be achieved on a clinical scanner for DKI exper-
iments within a reasonable TE. More recently, the oscillat-
ing gradient spin-echo (OGSE) sequence19–21 has also been
widely applied for frequency-specific diffusion encoding.
In OGSE, the diffusion-sensitizing gradients sinusoidally
oscillate, in which higher oscillation frequencies corre-
spond to lower effective diffusion times. Typically, OGSE
can probe shorter effective diffusion times than what is
achievable using PGSE. However, the reduced diffusion
encoding efficiency of OGSE compared to PGSE imposes
limitations for performing OGSE DKI experiments due to
gradient hardware constraints.21–23
Multiple studies have investigated the time and
frequency
dependence
of
kurtosis
using
preclinical
scanners.8,9,12,17,24–31 By combining OGSE and PGSE
experiments to mutually exclusively sample a wide range
of effective diffusion times, biphasic kurtosis time- and
frequency-dependences have been observed in rodent
brains in agreement with MC simulations, and the kurto-
sis time-dependence curve peaked at around 9 to 20 ms.9,24
Interestingly, a different study attempted to deploy both
OGSE and PGSE to probe similar effective diffusion times
and reported a disagreement in measured kurtosis values
from the two sequences in the rat hippocampus.17
Compared
to
the
relatively
rich
time-
and
frequency-dependent kurtosis data from MC simulations
and preclinical measurements, such data from clinical
scanners is rather sparse, especially over short diffusion
times because of hardware and scan time constraints. For
in vivo human measurements, monotonically decreasing
kurtosis with increasing diffusion time was reported in
cortical gray matter using PGSE with effective diffusion
times ranging from 21.2 to 100 ms.4 A similar trend was
also reported in tumors of patients with breast cancer30
and head and neck cancer32 over long effective diffusion
times (120 to 650 ms and 100 to 700 ms, respectively) using
STEAM-based techniques. A different study reported a
general decrease in kurtosis using a 23 Hz frequency-tuned
bipolar gradient compared to PGSE across the human
brain.33
Recent advances in gradient hardware34–38
have
enabled frequency-dependent kurtosis experiments of the
in vivo human brain using OGSE with higher oscillation
frequencies than were previously attainable. A recent
work sampled four frequencies (0, 18.4, 35.7, and 47.5 Hz)
using OGSE on a high-performance gradient system and
observed monotonically decreasing kurtosis with increas-
ing frequency (decreasing Δeff) in different parts of the
human brain.10 However, the non-monotonicity of kur-
tosis time-dependence has not yet been experimentally
demonstrated in the in vivo human brain.
In this work, we investigate the time and frequency
dependence of kurtosis in the human brain by combin-
ing OGSE sequences with four non-zero frequencies
(11, 20, 34, and 51 Hz) and PGSE sequences with three
effective diffusion times (50, 22.7, and 12.5 ms) on a
high-performance gradient system. Two OGSE–PGSE
sequence pairs are specifically designed to probe the
same effective diffusion times to explore how measured
kurtosis depends on the employed gradient waveform.

METHODS
2.1
Gradient waveforms
Four OGSE23,39 and three PGSE waveforms were utilized
in this study. The centroid frequencies23,39 of the four
OGSE waveforms were 11, 20, 34, and 51 Hz. The OGSE
waveforms were therefore abbreviated as OG11, OG20,
OG34, and OG51, respectively. Using a simple and com-
monly used Δeff-frequency conversion formula, Δeff =
1∕(4f), with f = ω∕(2π) being the centroid frequency of the
OGSE waveform,20 the corresponding effective diffusion
times of the four OGSE waveforms were 22.7, 12.5, 7.4,
and 4.9 ms, respectively. Based on the OGSE waveforms,
three PGSE waveforms were designed to have effective
diffusion times of 50, 22.7, and 12.5 ms, calculated using
Δeff = Δ −δ∕3.18 The PGSE waveforms were similarly
abbreviated as PG50, PG22.7, and PG12.5, respectively. As
such, OG11 and PG22.7 both probe an effective diffusion
time of 22.7 ms; OG20 and PG12.5 both probe an effec-
tive diffusion time of 12.5 ms. Gradient waveforms and
corresponding gradient moment power spectra are shown
in Figure 1.
2.2
In vivo brain imaging
In vivo human brain imaging experiments were carried out
on a Philips 3T Achieva system (Philips Healthcare, Best,
the Netherlands) equipped with a high-performance gra-
dient insert coil35 that can reach gradient amplitudes up to
200 mT/m and slew rates up to 600 mT/m/ms at 100% duty
cycle and a 1H–free transmit/receive quadrature birdcage
coil.40 The sequences used in this work required a lower
duty cycle such that the gradient amplitude limit could be
exceeded by up to 10%.
Seven healthy volunteers (four male, mean age
26.7 ± 3.1 years) were recruited for scanning in accor-
dance with local ethics policy. Over the experiments,
diffusion gradient waveforms described in Section 2.1
were employed with spiral readouts. For each sequence,
a
three-shell
acquisition
protocol
with
b-values
of
500, 1000, and 2000 s/mm2 was performed, with 16,
16, and 32 diffusion directions, respectively. Twelve
b = 0 image volumes were acquired for each sequence.

2.3
Field monitoring and image
reconstruction
All sequences were repeated after volunteer scanning to
monitor the spatiotemporal field dynamics during read-
out using a dynamic field camera based on 1H NMR
field probes41 (Skope Magnetic Resonance Technologies,
Zurich, Switzerland). Third-order spherical harmonic field
models, which were corrected for second-order concomi-
tant fields,42 were fitted to the field monitoring data and
used in conjunction with off-resonance maps in a higher
order algebraic reconstruction algorithm.43
2.4
Data analysis
Raw reconstructed image volumes were processed using
the DESIGNER pipeline.44,45 More specifically, magni-
tude data was first denoised,46 followed by Gibbs ring-
ing artifact removal,47 Rician bias correction,48 and bias
field correction.49 An in-house image intensity-based
rigid-body motion correction algorithm implemented in
MATLAB Release 2024a (MathWorks, Natick, MA) was
then applied to separately align all image volumes of
the same waveform measurement per volunteer. Finally,
image intensities were normalized based on b = 0 volumes
to reduce the impact of different receiver gains on signal
intensities across different b-value acquisitions of the same
waveform.45
Gradient nonlinearities, which are often worse in
high-performance gradient systems,50,51 cause spatially
varying b-tensors52 that deviate from their nominal spec-
ifications. To account for such deviations, a gradient
nonlinearity correction method53 was incorporated using
vendor-provided gradient field distributions per Cartesian
gradient axis of the employed high-performance gradient
insert coil. The resulting spatial b-tensor maps underwent
the same transformations as applied to the imaging data
for rigid-body motion correction.
Following gradient nonlinearity correction, kurtosis
tensors were fitted to preprocessed imaging data using
DESIGNER with constraints on positive kurtosis tensors,54
from which axial, mean, and radial kurtosis (AK, MK, and
RK, respectively) were extracted. Axial, mean, and radial
diffusivity (AD, MD, and RD, respectively) were similarly
extracted from the fitted diffusion tensor.
For tissue segmentation, all image volumes first
underwent brain extraction55
for better algorithmic
performance. T1-weighted anatomical volumes were
transformed to align with measured b = 0 volumes using
symmetric diffeomorphic image registration56 imple-
mented in ANTs (https://github.com/ANTsX/ANTs).57

Using the repeated measures analysis of variance
(ANOVA), the statistical significance of the overall time
and frequency dependence of kurtosis across all effective
diffusion times and frequencies was evaluated in each seg-
mented region. For regions with P < 0.05 in the repeated
measures ANOVA, additional paired-sample t-tests were
performed to assess the statistical significances of dif-
ferences between pairs of kurtosis measurements. More
specifically, within the four OG and the three PG measure-
ments of such regions, peak diffusion times with the high-
est kurtosis values were identified, and kurtosis at each
nonpeak diffusion time was compared to kurtosis at the
identified peak. The statistical significance of differences
in kurtosis measured at the same effective diffusion times
using OG and PG was also assessed using paired-sample
t-tests. All statistical tests were done separately for AK,
MK, and RK. P-values <0.05 were considered statistically
significant.
2.5
MC simulations
MC simulations were performed using Camino61,62 to
explore the impact of membrane permeability on time- and
frequency-dependent kurtosis measurements. The simu-
lation substrate was generated in a 2D cross-section of
35 × 35 μm2, containing 150 irregularly packed cylinders
with gamma-distributed radii. The gamma distribution of
cylinder radii was chosen to have a shape parameter of
1.55 and a scale parameter of 7 × 10−7 m, with resulting
mean cylinder radius, R, of 1.09 × 10−6 m; and intracellular
volume fraction, α, of 0.699 to mimic human WM.62
A total of 106 spins were randomly and uniformly ini-
tialized in intra- and extra-cellular spaces, with a free
diffusivity, D0, of 2 × 10−9 m2/s in both. Spin trajectories
were generated using eight different membrane transmis-
sion probabilities (p = [0, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8] × 10−3)
to simulate environments with different membrane per-
meabilities. All simulations had a constant time step, δt,
of 5 μs. The seed number was kept constant across the
eight spin trajectory generation processes to ensure iden-
tical substrate and spin initializations. The same diffusion
encoding schemes as described in Sections 2.1 and 2.2 were
applied for synthetic MRI signal generation. Kurtosis met-
rics were derived using the same algorithm as used for the
in vivo data.

DISCUSSION
Characterizing the evolution of kurtosis over different
diffusion times provides valuable information about the
underlying tissue microstructure being imaged. By com-
bining PGSE and OGSE waveforms to sample an extended
yet overlapping range of effective diffusion times and fre-
quencies using a high-performance gradient system, a
statistically significant non-monotonic, biphasic kurtosis
time- and frequency-dependence was observed for the first
time in the in vivo human brain. Moreover, discrepancies
in kurtosis values measured by OGSE and PGSE probing
the same effective diffusion times were observed.
For all WM and GM regions over long Δeff, kurto-
sis was observed to decrease with increasing Δeff. This
behavior arises due to water molecules having enough
time to explore different compartments of the diffusive
microenvironments, or said differently, water molecules
coarse-graining the underlying structural disorder5,6 and
exchanging between different compartments1,2,7,8 such
that the diffusion becomes increasingly Gaussian, with
less variability in diffusivity across different molecules.

As such, kurtosis asymptotically decreases to zero over
infinite Δeff, provided that all compartments are perme-
able, or to a non-zero value representing tissue hetero-
geneity over residual non-exchanging compartments.4,27
At shorter Δeff, kurtosis was observed to decrease with
decreasing Δeff in all regions. Over this regime, interac-
tions between water molecules and restrictions become
the dominant factor in kurtosis time- dependence.2 As Δeff
decreases, such interactions become increasingly scarce,
manifesting in decreasing kurtosis.9,10 Interestingly, at
51 Hz as compared to 11 Hz, kurtosis in WM regions exhib-
ited a greater reduction than in GM regions, illustrating a
faster approach toward Gaussian diffusion in WM regions,
which has also been reported in previous studies.10,33
With infinitely short Δeff, water molecules do not inter-
act with any restrictions, and each molecule undergoes
Gaussian diffusion.16 In the intermediate regime, the
interplay of abovementioned effects results in a turn-
ing point of the kurtosis time-dependence curve.16 Over-
all, the observed kurtosis trends in this study agree well
with previous PGSE kurtosis time-dependence4 and OGSE
kurtosis frequency-dependence10 results in the human
brain.
The peaks of the kurtosis time-dependence curves
were present at distinct effective diffusion times between
WM and GM regions. For MK and RK of most WM
regions, tpeak occurred at 22.7 ms. One exception is MK
of PLIC, which has the highest value at 50 ms, suggest-
ing that tpeak could be longer than the Δeff reached in
this study and, therefore, that a longer Δeff is required
to capture statistically significant non-monotonic kurto-
sis time-dependence in this region. Global GM exhibited
a tpeak ≤12.5 ms from PG measurements and ≥22.7 ms (or
equivalently, ≤11 Hz) from OG measurements that may
have not been reached by this study. This disagreement
in tpeak between PG and OG measurements for global
GM is likely due to differences in exchange sensitivity of
employed waveforms, as well as the heterogeneity of tissue
contained in global GM. RK of putamen had a clear peak at
34 Hz (7.4 ms), and MK of putamen and both RK and MK
of thalamus had clear peaks at 20 Hz (12.5 ms). The overall
shorter tpeak in GM regions than in WM regions suggests
faster exchange in the GM regions;12,16 this deduction is
corroborated by the MC simulations (Figure 7), for which
tpeak gradually becomes shorter as membrane transmis-
sion probability increases. Importantly, it should be noted
that because of the limited number of Δeff points being
sampled, the observed tpeak in this work does not corre-
spond to the exact Δeff where the peak occurs but rather the
range of Δeff over which the peak is located. For example,
a tpeak of 7.4 ms for putamen merely indicates that the kur-
tosis time-dependence curve for putamen reaches its peak
between 12.5 and 4.9 ms.
The observed non-monotonic time- and frequency-
dependent kurtosis suggests that both the short- and
long-time regimes of kurtosis are reached, with the
crossover regime principally occurring between 7.4 and
22.7 ms depending on the ROI.4 On the other hand, evi-
dence of the ω0.5 dependence of MD shown in Figure S4
as previously seen in 1D short-range disorder4,5,64 sug-
gests that diffusivity is likely in the long-time or crossover
regime at effective diffusion times down to 4.9 ms. Given
that the long-time limit of kurtosis starts at about four
times that of diffusivity,4 the crossover regime of diffusiv-
ity that can be expected based on observed kurtosis falls
in the range of 1.9–5.7 ms, which is consistent with the in
vivo findings. Similar results have also been reported in
previous work.10
Statistically significant discrepancies in kurtosis val-
ues measured using OGSE and PGSE waveforms that
were designed to probe the same effective diffusion times
were observed both in vivo and in MC simulations. Dif-
fusivities measured using OGSE and PGSE at the same
effective diffusion times show less prominent yet still
non-negligible discrepancies (Figure S5). One factor that
contributes to such discrepancies is the inadequacy of
the Δeff = 1∕(4f) conversion model between Δeff and
frequency. Despite being commonly used,9,17 the con-
vention is only approximate considering the nonlocal-
ity of the time–frequency conversion.6 Such inadequacy
explains discrepancies between simulated kurtosis of the
OG11–PG22.7 and OG20–PG12.5 pairs in the MC sim-
ulation without exchange (p = 0). Nonetheless, assigning
PGSE waveforms that have finite pulse durations to differ-
ent effective diffusion times and establishing a conversion
between Δeff and frequency provide more specificity than
generally ascribing PGSE measurements to 0 Hz.
In addition, the difference in flow sensitivity between
OG and PG waveforms (i.e., OG is flow-insensitive,
whereas PG is flow-sensitive) at the same Δeff could intro-
duce an additional difference in measured kurtosis and
requires further investigation. However, the presence of
similar discrepancies in MC simulations without flow sug-
gests that differences in flow sensitivity are unlikely to be
the main cause to the observed discrepancies.
An arguably more prominent effect that leads to
such discrepancies in kurtosis measurements is the dif-
ferences in exchange sensitivity of different gradient
waveforms,63 which was demonstrated by both MC sim-
ulations and theoretical predictions. As p increases (i.e.,
as the exchange rate increases), stronger exchange weight-
ing effects lead to smaller kurtosis. In our case, differ-
ences in exchange weightings between OG11 and PG22.7
and between OG20 and PG12.5 resulted in simulated
kurtosis differences, which were magnified with increas-
ing p (Figures 7 and 8). Indeed, GM regions that were

For a better depiction of the kurtosis time-dependence
curve and a better identification of tpeak, it is always desir-
able to sample a denser and wider range of effective dif-
fusion times and frequencies on a larger cohort. However,
scan time imposes an intrinsic limit on denser sampling
for in vivo human experiments. Currently, acquiring kur-
tosis measurement at seven effective diffusion times and
frequencies takes 53 minutes. An alternative to remain in
a feasible scan time while sampling even more time points
could be to utilize fast kurtosis imaging methods.67 On
the other hand, to sample a wider range of effective diffu-
sion times, longer effective diffusion times than achieved
in this work up to 800 ms have been demonstrated possi-
ble using PGSE and STEAM-based techniques on clinical
scanners.4,30,32 However, reaching higher frequencies for
OGSE comes at the cost of a prolonged TE under the same
gradient strengths due to the higher number of oscillation
periods needed to achieve the desired b-value.
To further disentangle different sources of kurtosis,
Q-space trajectory imaging decomposes the contributions
of tissue heterogeneity and microscopic anisotropy to
kurtosis into an isotropic and an anisotropic compo-
nent by combining linear and spherical tensor diffusion
encodings.68,69 As future work, OG and PG linear ten-
sor encoding waveforms can be employed together with
spherical tensor encoding waveforms that are optimized
for spectral selectivity and specificity70 to separately access
time- and frequency-dependent isotropic and anisotropic
kurtosis for an additional level of tissue microstructural
characterization.

CONCLUSION
A
non-monotonic,
biphasic
kurtosis
time-
and
frequency-dependence was observed for the first time
in the in vivo human brain by combining PGSE and
OGSE waveforms using a high-performance gradient
system. The observed kurtosis trends were attributed to
the combined effects of water-restriction interactions,
inter-compartmental water exchange, and tissue hetero-
geneity. In conjunction with MC simulations, the impact
of exchange on discrepancies between OG and PG kurtosis
measurements at the same effective diffusion times was
explored. The reported results demonstrated the study of
time- and frequency-dependent kurtosis as a sensitive tool
for characterizing brain microstructure.

Abstract: Purpose: To investigate the time and frequency dependence of diffusion kur- tosis in the in vivo human brain with pulsed (PGSE) and oscillating gradient spin-echo (OGSE) experiments over a range of diffusion times and frequencies using high-performance gradients. Methods: Four OGSE waveforms probing centroid frequencies of 11, 20, 34, and 51 Hz, corresponding to equivalent effective diffusion times of 22.7, 12.5, 7.4, and 4.9 ms; and three PGSE waveforms probing effective diffusion times of 50, 22.7, and 12.5 ms were designed for experimentation. Seven healthy volunteers were scanned using said waveforms at b-values of 500, 1000, and 2000 s/mm2. Kurtosis metrics were computed and evaluated in various white and gray matter regions of interest. Complementary Monte-Carlo simulations were performed using a simple substrate with varying permeabilities and the same gradient waveforms as used for in vivo imaging. Results: Non-monotonic, biphasic kurtosis time- and frequency-dependences were observed in different white and gray matter regions. This behavior supports the notion that kurtosis is influenced by the combined effects of water-restriction interactions, inter-compartmental water exchange, and tissue heterogeneity. Kurtosis values measured using OGSE and PGSE waveforms at the same effec- tive diffusion times showed significant discrepancies, with consistently higher values from PGSE than OGSE. These discrepancies are mainly attributed to differences in exchange sensitivities among gradient waveforms based on anal- ogous findings from Monte-Carlo simulations. Conclusion: Kurtosis was found to exhibit biphasic time- and frequency-dependence in the human brain. When interpreting kurtosis mea- surements, the influence of exchange sensitivities of employed gradient waveforms should be considered.
